listings.name: The Cargo Hold
listings.blurb: Dinner inside the bow of the Phantom Ship, with a shark tank for a dining-room wall.
body: Built into the hull of the Phantom Ship at uShaka Marine World, The Cargo Hold is the closest Durban gets to eating underwater. One wall of the restaurant is the viewing glass of the aquarium's shark tank, so ragged-tooth sharks drift past somewhere between your starter and your main.
The kitchen leans, sensibly, into seafood — line fish, prawns and a KwaZulu-Natal take on grilled catch. Ask for a tank-side table when you book; there are only a handful and they go first.
listings.address: uShaka Marine World, 1 Bell Street, Point

listings.name: Osteria 65
listings.blurb: Small Italian kitchen doing handmade pasta and a wine list that punches above the postcode.
body: Osteria 65 is the kind of restaurant that fills up on repeat customers. The menu is short, the pasta is rolled in-house, and the service knows the difference between attentive and hovering.
Go for the pasta of the day and let the floor staff pick the wine — they are unusually good at it.

listings.name: Butcher Block
listings.blurb: Aged steak, an open grill, and portions calibrated for people who skipped lunch.
body: A steakhouse that takes the butchery half of the name seriously — cuts are aged in-house and the day's selection is walked to the table before you order.
Book ahead on weekends. The Umhlanga room is busy from 19:00 and does not thin out early.

listings.name: The Ocean Terrace
listings.blurb: Breakfast, lunch and sundowners with the Umhlanga lighthouse in frame the whole way through.
body: The view does a lot of the work here, and the kitchen knows it — the menu is confident rather than clever, built around seafood, salads and a properly good breakfast.
Sundowners on the terrace are the move. Arrive by 17:00 in summer if you want a railing table.

listings.name: Café 1999
listings.blurb: Long-running Mediterranean tapas spot that helped teach Durban to share plates.

listings.name: Little Gujarat
listings.blurb: Quarter mutton bunny that settles arguments. Cash-friendly, queue-forming, no frills.
body: There is a version of the Durban curry argument that ends at this counter. The bunny chow is the reason to come: a quarter loaf, hollowed, filled and handed over hot.
Do not expect atmosphere. Expect the food to be right.

listings.name: Freedom Café
listings.blurb: A shipping-container coffee bar off Florida Road with breakfast worth the wait for a table.

listings.name: Unity Brasserie & Bar
listings.blurb: Florida Road's reliable all-nighter — kitchen until late, upstairs bar later still.

listings.name: Spiga d'Oro
listings.blurb: Pavement tables, pasta at midnight, and thirty years of Florida Road people-watching.

listings.name: The Chairman
listings.blurb: Live jazz in a restored harbour building. Dress up a little; it suits the room.

listings.name: The Green Mango
listings.blurb: Plant-based cooking that doesn't apologise for itself, in the middle of student Glenwood.

listings.name: Afro's & Arabs
listings.blurb: Halaal grills and mezze with a menu that reads like a road trip up the east coast.

listings.name: The Oyster Box
listings.blurb: The lighthouse hotel. Curry buffet, black-and-white tiles, and a view that never gets old.
body: Umhlanga's landmark hotel sits directly opposite the lighthouse, close enough that the beach is a walk rather than a drive. It is unashamedly grand — a colonial-era building restored with more colour than restraint.
Even if you are not staying, two things are worth booking: high tea, and the curry buffet at the Ocean Terrace. Both fill weeks ahead in season.

listings.name: Beverly Hills Hotel
listings.blurb: Umhlanga's original high-rise beach hotel, with balconies aimed straight at the Indian Ocean.

listings.name: Southern Sun Elangeni & Maharani
listings.blurb: Two towers on the beachfront promenade — the practical choice for a Golden Mile weekend.

listings.name: Hilton Durban
listings.blurb: Across the road from the ICC. The default when the trip is work, not sand.

listings.name: Teremok Marine
listings.blurb: Nine-room boutique lodge a street back from the beach. Quiet, green, adults-leaning.

listings.name: Coco de Mer
listings.blurb: Guest house pricing, sea-facing rooms, and breakfast on a deck above the dunes.

listings.name: Ballito Beach Apartments
listings.blurb: Self-catering flats within walking distance of Willard Beach — built for families who cook.

listings.name: The Benjamin
listings.blurb: On Florida Road, above the noise. Walk to dinner, walk home again.

listings.name: uShaka Marine World
listings.blurb: Africa's largest aquarium bolted onto a wet-and-wild water park. Budget a full day.
body: uShaka splits into Sea World — the aquarium, dolphin and seal presentations — and Wet 'n Wild, the slide park next door. Combination tickets cover both, and you will need most of a day to do either properly.
Arrive at opening in school holidays. The queues for the big slides build fast after 11:00.

listings.name: Moses Mabhida SkyCar & Big Swing
listings.blurb: Ride the arch for the city's best viewpoint, or jump off it if that's your temperament.
listings.address: Moses Mabhida Stadium, Isaiah Ntshangase Road

listings.name: Durban Botanic Gardens
listings.blurb: Africa's oldest surviving botanic garden. Free, shaded, and full of Sunday picnickers.

listings.name: The Golden Mile Promenade
listings.blurb: Eight kilometres of paved beachfront. Run it, cycle it, or just watch Durban go past.
listings.address: Snell Parade to uShaka, Durban Beachfront

listings.name: Umgeni River Bird Park
listings.blurb: A cliff-side aviary park with waterfalls and a free-flight bird show at 11:00 and 14:00.

listings.name: Phansi Museum
listings.blurb: A Victorian house packed with southern African beadwork, baskets and ceremonial dress.

listings.name: Mitchell Park
listings.blurb: Small zoo, big lawns, a tea garden, and the safest toddler afternoon in the city.

listings.name: Durban Street Food & Spice Tour
listings.blurb: Victoria Street Market, the spice traders, and four stops you would never find alone.

listings.name: Addington Tidal Pool
listings.blurb: Flat, sheltered saltwater swimming for days when the backline is doing too much.

listings.name: Zimbali Spa
listings.blurb: Forest-canopy treatment rooms forty minutes up the coast. Book the half-day package.

listings.name: Gateway Theatre of Shopping
listings.blurb: One of the largest malls in the southern hemisphere. Wear comfortable shoes.

listings.name: Victoria Street Market
listings.blurb: Spices by the scoop, curios by the aisle. Haggling expected, not resented.

listings.name: I Heart Market
listings.blurb: First-Saturday design market where Durban's makers actually stand behind their own tables.

listings.name: Essenwood Market
listings.blurb: Saturday morning under the trees — plants, pastries, records and a lot of catching up.

listings.name: Corner Store Glenwood
listings.blurb: Ceramics, prints and homeware from KZN studios, in a shop the size of a lounge.

listings.name: Adams Booksellers
listings.blurb: Trading since 1865 and still the best African-history shelf in the province.

listings.name: Blue Security
listings.blurb: Armed response and monitoring across the greater Durban area, 24/7.

listings.name: Coastal Plumbing Co.
listings.blurb: Licensed plumbers covering the Berea, Westville and the Highway area. Same-day callouts.

listings.name: Mangwanani African Spa
listings.blurb: Half-day and full-day African spa packages, with branches up and down the coast.

listings.name: Umhlanga Auto Care
listings.blurb: Independent servicing and diagnostics that keeps your warranty intact.

listings.name: Harbour Accounting
listings.blurb: Small-business accounting, SARS submissions and payroll for Durban owner-operators.

listings.name: East Coast Events
listings.blurb: Weddings, launches and conferences — staging, sound and the permits nobody enjoys.

events.title: Durban Night Market
events.blurb: Three nights of food trucks, makers and live sets on the lawns beside the beach.
body: The night market takes over Suncoast Park for a long weekend three times a year: around sixty traders, a stage at the far end, and enough seating that you are not eating standing up.
Entry is free before 18:00. Bring a card — most traders have moved off cash.

events.title: Gagasi FM Summer Concert
events.blurb: The station's flagship summer line-up, with local headliners and a full stadium stage.

events.title: Sushi & Gin Festival
events.blurb: Forty gin producers, unlimited sushi, and a very sensible shuttle arrangement.

events.title: Comrades Marathon
events.blurb: The world's oldest ultramarathon finishes in the city. Road closures from 04:00.

events.title: Vodacom Durban July
events.blurb: Africa's biggest horse-racing day, and the only fashion brief Durban takes seriously.

events.title: Durban International Film Festival
events.blurb: Eleven days of African cinema across Suncoast, the Playhouse and campus screens.

events.title: I Heart Market
events.blurb: Durban's monthly design market — 150 makers, one morning, no resellers.

events.title: Umhlanga Summer Sundowners
events.blurb: Acoustic sets on the village green from 17:00, with the lighthouse doing the lighting.

posts.title: How to eat a bunny chow without embarrassing yourself
posts.author: I Love Durban
posts.excerpt: There is a right way, several acceptable ways, and one way that will get you talked about after you leave.
body: A bunny chow is a quarter, half or full loaf of white bread, hollowed out and filled with curry. The bread you remove — the virgin — is not a garnish. It is the spoon, and it is also the last bite.

Start at a corner, not the middle. Pull the virgin apart in pieces small enough to hold curry without collapsing, and work inwards. The loaf's walls will soften as you go; that is the point, and it is why a bunny is eaten in one sitting rather than carried around.
Cutlery is not forbidden, but nobody who grew up on these is reaching for it. Order a quarter mutton the first time. If you finish it and want more, you have learned something about yourself.

posts.title: Durban's beaches, ranked by what you actually want from a beach
posts.author: I Love Durban
posts.excerpt: Swimming, surfing, running, or sitting still while somebody else supervises the children — different beaches, all of them ours.
body: The Golden Mile is not one beach, it is eight kilometres of them, and the differences matter more than the map suggests.

For flat water and lifeguards, Addington's tidal pool is the safest bet in the city. For surfing, head to the piers at North Beach. For a run, take the promenade at 06:00 before the heat arrives. For families, uShaka Beach puts the aquarium, the toilets and the ice cream within one radius.
All of them are warm all year. That is the part visitors never quite believe until they are in it.

posts.title: 48 hours in Durban, done properly
posts.author: I Love Durban
posts.excerpt: A weekend itinerary that does not involve driving in circles on the M4.
body: Friday evening: check in around Umhlanga, walk to the lighthouse for sunset, eat within walking distance so the car stays where it is.
Saturday: the botanic gardens early, Victoria Street Market for spice and lunch, the SkyCar at Moses Mabhida in the late afternoon, and dinner on Florida Road.
Sunday: uShaka if you have children, the promenade if you do not. Leave the curry buffet for the last meal — it is the one you will describe when you get home.

posts.title: What 'support local' actually means for a Durban business
posts.author: I Love Durban
posts.excerpt: Spoiler: the review you leave is worth more to a small business than the R40 you spent.
body: Small businesses in this city do not lose to competitors nearly as often as they lose to invisibility. A restaurant with no photographs, no hours and no reviews may be the best kitchen in Glenwood, and nobody will find out.
The two things that move the needle cost nothing: leave the review, and tell the owner where you heard about them. Both of those change what they invest in next.
